evidence: Word-by-word against SOURCE.txt. Replaced words: "Read it out loud as you're writing it. Long, elegant sentences don't read well when you're being induced. It's all just soup." Draft: "And then read it out loud as you write it. Long, elegant sentences are NOT going to help you when you’re trying to induce. It’s all soup to you at that point." Sentence 1 keeps the instruction (read it aloud while writing) and adds "And then", a sequence word that matches the guide's own "then read the script aloud" and follows the sentence before it (think about the verb, quality, refrain, transition). Sentence 2 keeps "Long, elegant sentences" and the warning, with three shifts: (a) "don't read well" becomes "are NOT going to help you" (readability becomes usefulness; the soup sentence after it carries the guide's actual claim); (b) the caps NOT adds emphasis that neither the guide nor the replaced words have (the writer's own D9 note calls it Emulate's turn); (c) "when you're being induced" (the receiver) becomes "when you’re trying to induce" (the doer, with an attempt in it). On (c): this is a real change in who is doing what, but in a self-hypnosis guide the reader is both, the guide's own wording is the neutral "during an induction", and the sentence after it ("soup to you at that point") puts the experience back on the person in the induction, so I read it as the same time frame and the same advice, not a different one. Sentence 3 drops "just" and adds "to you at that point", which names the person and moment that "become soup during an induction" already implies; no new claim. I weighed (a) to (c) against 'no more, no less': they change emphasis and viewpoint, not what is advised (read aloud while writing; long elegant sentences are a problem in the induction; they turn to soup), and they add no claim, condition, person or number. The guide's meaning ("read the script aloud; long elegant sentences become soup during an induction") is all present, and nothing of his is left out (the pick-one-verb-quality-refrain-transition part is in the sentence before and untouched). Notes for the writer, not draft faults: the_change says Emulate's three sentences (sample cn) with no put-back fix, and the draft is those sentences, but its gloss ("don't help in an induction", "soup then") is looser than the real words ("when you're trying to induce", "soup to you at that point"), and (b) and (c) are changes from wording the writer calls approved, so the card should show the real words as changes; the T14 and T15 ledger lines in ADMISSION.json say the draft 'puts back' a point Emulate dropped, which I cannot see in this draft, and I did not rely on them; the draft's two apostrophes (you’re, It’s) are curly while the rest of that paragraph and the replaced words are straight (cosmetic). CONTEXT.txt holds the three sentences once, as the end of the third paragraph and of the section, and they read right there. TELLS: I went through T01-T29 and C01-C04 on the draft in its context and find none PRESENT. Closest calls: T20 and T29 (the last line "It’s all soup to you at that point.") - it closes the paragraph as the replaced "It's all just soup." did, and it carries the guide's image, which the sentence before it does not say ('not going to help' is weaker than 'soup'), so cutting it would lose a claim; it is not a 'So...' summary or a moral; T02 and T09 - the paragraph runs instruction, instruction, warning, image, but that is the guide's own order, the sentences differ in length and type, and the swap adds no step; T15 - the phrases differ over the same three-beat structure, but they are changes of viewpoint and voice, not rarer synonyms for their own sake; T16 and T18 - 'NOT ... It's all soup' is not a 'not X, it's Y' contrast and the soup line does not flip a premise; T07 - 'And then' and the caps NOT are a sequence word and an emphasis, not hesitations or fillers; C02 - 'it' is the script from 'When you're writing this' and 'that point' is 'when you’re trying to induce'. LINTER: "B7 short landing at paragraph end" ("It’s all soup to you at that point.") - accepted: same role and position as the replaced closing line, his own image, and 'at that point' places it rather than sums up. "D9 follows the source order" - accepted: an in-place swap that keeps the guide's order (read aloud, long sentences, soup); T13 and T09 are answered above. "E36/E41 heavy second person" (12.5 'you' per 100 words = 4 in 32 words) - accepted: the replaced words have 2 in 22 (9.1) and the draft adds 'help you' and 'to you'; both are the practitioner as object and experiencer of the induction in a how-to paragraph, there is no generic scenery (E36), and the voice is blunt, not reassuring (E41).
